study.title: Ezekiel 15 The useless vine and judgment on Jerusalem
study.overview: This chapter uses the image of the wood of the vine to show that Jerusalem, though chosen by God, had become unproductive and unable to serve for any noble use. The argument of the text is direct: if the wood of the vine is already useless when it is intact, the more it was burned; so also Jerusalem, because of its infidelity, would be judged. The focus is not lacking in God's worth, but on loss of utility because of persistent transgression. The chapter concludes with the assertion that the land would be made in desolation for having committed great infidelity.

outline.title: The question about the wood of the vine
outline.explanation: The Lord begins with a provocative comparison: the wood of the vine is not better than other woods or serves for useful work. The image prepares the reader to understand that Jerusalem was not being judged by chance, but because it had become spiritually unprofitable.

outline.title: The uselessness of the vine even before and after the fire
outline.explanation: The text insists that not even the whole vine serves to manufacture something useful, much less after burning. The metaphor reinforces that the judgment is not excessive: the wood was already unfit for any work, and the fire only shows this condition.

outline.title: Application of the image to Jerusalem and the final sentence
outline.explanation: God applies the figure to the inhabitants of Jerusalem: as the vine delivered to the fire, they would suffer divine judgment. Even those who escaped one fire would fall into another, and the land would be left in desolation because of the great unfaithfulness of the people.

study.context: The given notes place this chapter within a sequence of metaphors in Ezekiel which announce, from various angles, the certainty of the judgment on Jerusalem. They also mention, in interpretive language, that the previous fall of Judah and the future destruction of Jerusalem are seen as stages of this judgment. The biblical text, however, focuses on the image of the vine and moral guilt of the people, not in extensive historical details.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the election of Jerusalem did not nullify moral responsibility. The image of the vine highlights that external value, religious identity or privileged position are not enough when there is no fidelity to the Lord. Judgment is presented as just and unavoidable because the people broke the covenant through serious transgression. The truth also appears that partially escaping from a discipline does not mean being free from it; whoever persists in unfaithfulness finds God's judgment in an increasing way. By saying that the earth would be made desolate, the text links sin, alliance and historical consequence directly.

scholarViews.insight: Jerusalem is compared to the vine without value: as vine wood, the people are useless for any work and their unfaithfulness breaks the covenant, resulting in desolation.

The destruction of Jerusalem is presented as as necessary as cutting and throwing into the fire the dead branches of a vine; the prophet receives the explanation that there was no remedy for this judgment.
The wood of the vine is useless because the vine has only value for its fruit; thus, Israel is described as good for nothing but to fulfill the purpose of God.

questions: What signs of spiritual utility can exist outwardly without true fruit before God?
How does the image of the burnt vine correct the idea that a small escape from judgment means divine approval?
In what ways can infidelity God make life and community spiritually desolate today?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to examine whether his life is producing real fruit of fidelity, and not just religious appearance. Concrete application is to abandon any trust in empty spiritual privileges and turn to the Lord with sincere repentance, for mere existence in the community of faith does not replace obedience. It also invites us to take God's discipline seriously before sterility becomes desolation.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are limited and do not bring detailed comments to each verse; therefore, some historical and theological connections have been maintained at a moderate level and only when supported by the text itself and the received excerpts. The exact date and the broader historical sequence of the judgment were not developed beyond what the notes mention.
